examples.scenario: A composite tile is published in 2022 and code records 2022 as the survey date.
examples.reason: The composite contains surveys spanning many years; the location-specific survey index must supply the contributing survey date.

examples.scenario: The newest downloadable file is assumed to contain the newest survey at the target location.
examples.reason: File publication/download time is not the airborne acquisition date.

examples.scenario: A Phase 3 National LIDAR Programme block is assumed to be newer than every Phase 2 block nationally.
examples.reason: Phase numbering is repeat lineage within a block; exact survey dates must come from metadata.

examples.scenario: A point-cloud ground return differs from the time-stamped DTM cell and replaces it.
examples.reason: Environment Agency documents that final DTM manual editing can make ground-class points differ from the derived DTM.

examples.scenario: No matching point cloud exists for a historic DTM survey, so the DTM is discarded.
examples.reason: Historic archiving means not every raster surface model necessarily has a matching point cloud.

examples.scenario: A 10m composite cell is used because it covers the parcel even though native 1m time-stamped DTM exists.
examples.reason: The 10m product is bilinearly resampled from the 2m composite and is more derived than native survey-resolution DTM.

examples.scenario: A DSM tile has the right survey date and is used for terrain height.
examples.reason: DSM includes buildings, vegetation and other surface objects; terrain requires DTM.

examples.scenario: A retired 2020 composite is selected because its local file path appears before the current composite.
examples.reason: Retired generations are historical provenance references, not the preferred current source.

examples.scenario: Two survey-index features intersect the target location and the first returned feature is accepted silently.
examples.reason: Multiple matches require explicit overlap/date/resolution reconciliation rather than API return order.

examples.scenario: The survey index returns no feature and code falls back to the composite publication year.
examples.reason: Missing location-specific lineage cannot be replaced with a dataset-level year.

examples.scenario: The exact survey ID is known but its transformation/geoidal model is omitted.
examples.reason: Time-stamped metadata explicitly records transformation and geoidal-model context.

examples.scenario: A survey start date is newer but its end date is older because fields were swapped.
examples.reason: Survey start/end chronology must be validated before lineage is accepted.

examples.scenario: A composite uses a newer coarse survey instead of an older finer survey and code assumes the rule is always newest-only.
examples.reason: Environment Agency describes the composite rule as newest, best-resolution data; the exact contributing survey must come from the index.

examples.scenario: Adjacent composite cells come from different survey years but are treated as one acquisition epoch.
examples.reason: Composite coverage can mix contributing surveys and must retain per-location lineage.

examples.scenario: A National LIDAR Programme block ID is stored but its phase is dropped.
examples.reason: Repeat captures reuse the block concept with incrementing phase numbers.

examples.scenario: Only the phase number is stored without survey dates.
examples.reason: Phase numbering is not a substitute for acquisition-date metadata.

examples.scenario: A point-cloud tile from the same year is assumed to be the source of the DTM tile.
examples.reason: Year coincidence does not prove raster derivation lineage, especially for historical archives.

examples.scenario: A 25cm retired composite is preferred solely because its nominal resolution is finer than current products.
examples.reason: Product status, acquisition lineage and current authoritative policy outrank nominal resolution alone.

examples.scenario: A survey index is queried with a buffered parcel and the buffer intersects an extra survey polygon.
examples.reason: Lineage must be tied to the exact query geometry used for the target parcel/location.

examples.scenario: The same survey-index query later returns a different feature set but no digest is stored.
examples.reason: Reproducible lineage requires recording the exact returned feature set.

examples.scenario: A current composite and retired composite point to different source surveys at the same location.
examples.reason: Composite generations can change source selection; the active dataset identity must be pinned.

examples.scenario: A composite tile is downloaded without its survey-index metadata and is treated as self-describing.
examples.reason: The tile alone does not encode the complete location-specific contributing-survey history.

examples.scenario: A time-stamped DTM tile is known but its survey date metadata is missing.
examples.reason: Time-stamped selection requires explicit acquisition-date provenance.

examples.scenario: A survey has a matching date but a different resolution from the tile being sampled.
examples.reason: Tile resolution is part of the exact survey-product binding.

examples.scenario: A tile lineage manifest records survey ID but not tile byte digest.
examples.reason: Exact provenance binds immutable raster bytes to the survey metadata record.

examples.scenario: A tile byte digest matches but its linked survey ID changes on replay.
examples.reason: Same bytes with different claimed lineage are not an auditable terminal record.

examples.scenario: Independent lineage replay finds the same survey date but a different survey feature ID.
examples.reason: Date equality alone does not prove the same source survey.

examples.scenario: Survey-index WFS and downloaded index disagree on the target feature set.
examples.reason: Independent index channels must be reconciled before terminal binding.

examples.scenario: Static survey-lineage QA completes while canonical point rows remain zero.
examples.reason: Lineage guards can advance without fabricating coordinates or elevation values.

examples.scenario: Missing runner ACK is bypassed by launching a second survey-lineage runner.
examples.reason: The continuation contract requires the existing single shared runner.

examples.scenario: Known execution blockers are changed to pending to make the dashboard look active.
examples.reason: Known unresolved execution conditions remain blocked; pending stays zero.

examples.scenario: Batch 73 is reported as a measured parcel height result.
examples.reason: Real height difference still requires canonical points, exact parcel boundary, immutable DTM tile, survey-lineage binding, execution, sampling and readback.
